newsitem.title: INDIA: Signs of political deal for new India government.
newsitem.headline: Signs of political deal for new India government.

text.p: India's defeated coalition showed signs of moving towards a deal with its ally-turned-foe Congress party on Saturday to find a new government after the fall of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.

A close aide of a key political negotiator in Deve Gowda's 15-party United Front told Reuters that the alliance had in its internal talks shown a willingness to consider replacing its leader to make peace with the Congress party.
"There is no other way," the aide, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters as the decision-making Steering Committee of the centre-left United Front held a meeting.

Deve Gowda resigned on Friday after his coalition was defeated in parliament in a confidence vote after the Congress withdrew vital support and refused to resume backing his alliance unless it changed its leader.
The United Front has so far refused to yield, and says the alliance is speaking with one voice.
President Shankar Dayal Sharma asked Deve Gowda to remain as caretaker prime minister while efforts were made to forge a new governing majority in the hung parliament.
The front was still weighing its options, and there were differences within the coalition, the aide said.
"Deve Gowda says they (the alliance) can do well in an election. But there are others in the United Front who do not want a mid-term poll," he said.
As a last effort to avert a mid-term poll, a change of leadership could be considered, he said.

"I don't see any rhyme or reason for the Congress decision to withdraw support to the government. So we have no other way out but to go for the mandate of the people," the Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted Deve Gowda as saying in a television report.
Deve Gowda appeared to carry weight in the coalition.

"It (the alliance) was united yesterday. It is united today," Ram Vilas Paswan, railway minister in the defeated cabinet, told reporters outside the prime minister's house. "We have said from the beginning that Deve Gowda is our leader."
The 10-month-old government was formed last June by the alliance, which has 178 lawmakers, with support from the Congress, which has 140 deputies in the 545-member lower house.

They closed ranks last year to oust a 12-day-old government formed by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which controls 193 deputies. The groups accuse the BJP of favouring majority Hindus over the Moslem minority.
Congress president Sitaram Kesri accused Deve Gowda of not containing the BJP when he withdrew his party's support to him, but is widely seen as having made a personal bid for power.
The Congress party, keen to sidestep early elections, said on Saturday it had no plans to seek power and reiterated it would support the United Front if it replaced Deve Gowda.
"If they come up with a new leader, we will support them," Congress spokesman Ved Prakash told Reuters. "We will not press our claim to form the government."
Kesri said his first priority was to avoid polls that could ensue if the United Front and Congress failed to agree on a successor to Deve Gowda, PTI reported.

All political formations agreed on Friday to try to approve the 1997/98 (April-March) budget in a special sitting of parliament from April 21 to 23. That would give politicians almost two weeks to resolve differences over a new government.
Parliament speaker P.A. Sangma on Saturday met President Sharma on the special budget session, and his spokesman said Sharma agreed to help move the budget for consideration in parliament.
